The library was closing, but the rain had other plans. It gathered at the windows in bright, hurried lines, turning every streetlamp into a small, wavering fire. People lingered between the shelves, pretending to read spines while listening to the weather. No one wanted to be the first to open an umbrella.

Near the returns cart, a boy held a book against his chest. He had that private look people wear when a story has followed them out of its pages. Beside him, an old woman wound her scarf twice around her neck and smiled at no one in particular.

I thought about how many rooms exist inside an ordinary evening: the room of the body, tired and warm; the room of memory, rearranging its furniture; the room of anticipation, already standing tomorrow’s kettle on the stove. Then there is the smallest room, the present, which we keep leaving because it seems too plain.

Yet the present was not plain. A radiator ticked. Somewhere, a chair sighed across the floor. The librarian switched off half the lights, and the remaining shelves glowed like houses on a distant hill.

When the doors finally opened, cool air carried in the smell of pavement and leaves. We stepped outside together, strangers under a dark, enormous ceiling. For one block, our separate umbrellas moved in the same direction. And somehow, without speaking, we had become a shelter, though none of us noticed until later. Then we turned away, each carrying a little weather home.
